composite.source: NWS fullSnow entry identifies ice-crystal precipitation mainly branched; fullgrowth paragraph explains branches. Rain liquid and hail compact ice differ; RussianWetSnow names a mixed or melting state.
composite.editorial: Branching structure identifies the general precipitation form Snow; WetSnow is a plausible subtype/mixed state but not a second equivalent definition of this form. No snow-root in prompt; key length4 matches Hail4, labels parallel. Key0 and easy preserved.

explanation.source: Snowentry directly supports agglomeration; growth paragraph supports temperature-dependent branching and sticking.
explanation.editorial: Aggregation and growth conditions explain more than identifying Snow; often prevents an all-crystals aggregation claim.

note0.source: Direct vapor deposition and branched crystals explicitly supported by NWS. Descriptive statement about individual crystals does not say all crystals always branch.
note0.editorial: Vapor origin adds a mechanism beyond the prompt structural clue; useful feedback for the correct choice.

note1.source: CompleteRain andDrizzle entries give strict diameter boundaries >0.5mm and <0.5mm.
note1.editorial: Attributed contrast teaches the sizes of two liquid precipitation forms, not a bare wrong-answer negation.

note2.source: CompleteHail entry says irregular pellets or balls of ice.
note2.editorial: Compact particle structure is informative about Hail and distinguishes its plausible ice distractor.

note3.source: CompleteRussian table row says simultaneous snow/rain, snow predominates; USsleet is not substituted.
note3.editorial: Mixed precipitation provides positive useful feedback and explains why this offered subtype does not best name the general branching-crystal form.
